questions.q: In the cell biology context of this course, what is Actin?
options: The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
The division of the nucleus, in which the replicated chromosomes separate.
One of the two proteins of the contractile ring, which pinches the cell into two; it is also the track along which cargo is carried inside the cell.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
questions.why: Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in the cell: during division it joins myosin to form the contractile ring, tightening like a rope from the centre of the cell and dividing the cytoplasm in two; the rest of the time it is the track of the cytoskeleton, along which vesicles and organelles are carried away by motor proteins; it is also the scaffold of the whole cell's shape, so the migration and invasion of cancer cells depend almost entirely on laying down new actin networks. The other three describe the nucleolus, mitosis and the lysosome.

questions.q: In the anaphase of mitosis, what actually happens inside the cell?
options: The centromeres of the sister chromatids separate, each set is pulled by the spindle fibres towards opposite poles, and the cell is elongated as a result.
The step that splits the cytoplasm into two after mitosis.
The receiving end of the Golgi apparatus, where incoming vesicles dock.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
questions.why: The earlier part of the division cycle is prophase (assembly of the spindle, condensation of the chromosomes) and metaphase (the chromosomes lining up on the equatorial plate), and then comes anaphase: the centromeres of the sister chromatids separate, each set is pulled by the spindle fibres towards opposite poles, and the cell is elongated; only when anaphase ends do you move on to telophase, when the nuclear envelope is rebuilt. This stage matters because the separation of the chromosomes and the division of the cytoplasm are two mutually independent events. The other three describe cytokinesis, the receiving end of the Golgi apparatus and the nucleolus.

questions.q: What is the function of APAF-1?
options: The control room. It keeps the DNA and decides which genes are read.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
The packaging room. It sorts finished proteins and sends them to their destinations.
The adaptor protein that brings cytochrome c and procaspase-9 together to form the apoptosome.
questions.why: Once the mitochondrion releases cytochrome c, these proteins meet in the cytoplasm, and APAF-1 is the protein that does the recruiting: it changes shape on binding cytochrome c, then pulls procaspase-9 in to assemble a wheel-shaped apoptosome, which activates caspase-9. Without APAF-1, cytochrome c would simply drift in the cytoplasm, the apoptosome could not be assembled, and caspase-9 would never be activated. The other three describe the nucleus, the lysosome and the Golgi apparatus.

questions.q: Compared with necrosis, what is the fundamental difference between apoptosis and other forms of cell death in the way the cell dies and in the consequences?
options: Uncontrolled cell death after injury, in which the contents leak out and cause inflammation in the surrounding tissue.

The cell packages its own contents into apoptotic bodies, cuts itself into fragments and lets phagocytes clear them away; the plasma membrane stays broadly intact, so the process causes no inflammation.
The part of the endoplasmic reticulum that carries ribosomes, where new proteins are made and folded.
The cell eats up the parts it does not need, in exchange for nutrients.
questions.why: There are two kinds of cell death: apoptosis is regulated, with the cell packaging its own contents into apoptotic bodies, cutting itself into fragments and letting phagocytes clear them away, the plasma membrane staying broadly intact so that no inflammation is triggered; necrosis, by contrast, is the accidental rupture that follows injury, in which leaking contents cause inflammation. Apoptosis has an intrinsic and an extrinsic initiation route, and both converge on caspase 3; tumours often survive precisely by shutting this gate off. The other three describe necrosis, the rough ER and autophagy.

questions.q: After cytochrome c is released into the cytoplasm, it assembles into a wheel-shaped complex that pulls procaspase-9 in and activates it. What is the English name of this wheel-shaped complex?
options: Caspase
APAF-1
Apoptosome
Bcl-2 family
questions.why: This “wheel” is the apoptosome: cytochrome c and APAF-1 bind, self-assemble into a heptameric wheel-shaped structure, pull procaspase-9 in and activate it, and caspase 9 then cleaves procaspase 3, so the execution phase begins; it is one of the very few giant structures that assemble themselves from cytoplasmic proteins. The other three are respectively the enzyme that cleaves proteins, the adaptor protein that makes up the apoptosome, and the group of proteins that decides whether the mitochondrion releases the apoptotic signal.

questions.q: In a nutrient-poor environment (for example the hypoxic core of a solid tumour), what role does autophagy play for tumour cells?
options: It packages unwanted organelles and proteins into autophagosomes, sends them to the lysosome for breakdown and recycles the amino acids and energy to stay alive, which makes it a survival strategy.
Programmed cell death: the cell takes itself apart neatly instead of bursting.
The organelle that organises microtubules and forms the spindle.
The outer skin of the cell. A lipid bilayer that controls what enters and leaves and carries receptors.
questions.why: When nutrients run short the cell switches on autophagy: it packages unwanted organelles and proteins into autophagosomes, sends them to the lysosome for breakdown, and uses the recovered amino acids and energy to stay alive. Seen from the tumour's point of view this is a survival strategy, which is why in the third lecture, on cancer progression, he specifically points out that the “promotion phase” comes with a rise in autophagy, a rise in angiogenesis and a fall in immune homeostasis. Therapeutically it cuts both ways: inhibiting autophagy can starve a tumour that depends on it, but it can also let the survivors of treatment live on. The other three describe programmed cell death, the organising centre of the spindle and the outer skin of the cell.

questions.q: Two parties stand on the outer mitochondrial membrane deciding the fate of the cell: the anti-apoptotic members hold the membrane and stop cytochrome c leaking out, while the pro-apoptotic members puncture it so that it is released. This family is called ______.
options: The space between the two mitochondrial membranes, where protons accumulate to drive ATP synthase.
The ectoderm. It becomes the skin and the nervous system.
A protein whose level rises and falls during the cell cycle and switches on the matching CDK; it is the key, not the machine.
The group of proteins that decides whether the mitochondrion releases the apoptotic signal.
questions.why: Members of the Bcl-2 family stand on two sides of the outer mitochondrial membrane: the anti-apoptotic members (Bcl-2 itself, for instance) guard the membrane and prevent cytochrome c from leaking out; the pro-apoptotic members (bak and bax, for instance) puncture the membrane so that cytochrome c is released, then assembles the apoptosome and activates caspase 9. The clinical application is the bispecific antibody that hits TRAILR2 and CDH17 at the same time. The other three describe the intermembrane space of the mitochondrion, the ectoderm and cyclin.

questions.q: What is BI 905711?
options: The receiving end of the Golgi apparatus, where incoming vesicles dock.
A tetrahedral bispecific antibody that recognises TRAILR2 and CDH17 at the same time.
The state in which normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA are mixed together inside one cell.
The part of the cell cycle in which DNA is replicated.
questions.why: BI 905711 is his own research example: a single molecule that recognises two targets at once, one being the death receptor TRAILR2 that triggers apoptosis, the other being CDH17, which appears only on the surface of cancer cells; it attacks only when both are present, which is the AND-gate design in the glossary, used to solve the problem of “killing normal cells”. The other three describe the receiving end of the Golgi apparatus, the mixed state of mitochondrial DNA and the DNA replication phase.

questions.q: Once the extrinsic pathway of apoptosis has been triggered, caspase-8 cleaves bid, and the tbid that is cut out goes to the mitochondrion to promote the release of cytochrome c. What is the English name of the protein that is cut?
options: Caspase
tbid
bid
Cytochrome c
questions.why: The extrinsic and intrinsic pathways of apoptosis begin as two separate roads, but once caspase-8 has been activated the extrinsic route cleaves bid, and the tbid that is cut out travels to the mitochondrial membrane and promotes the release of cytochrome c, joining the two roads; in other words, a death signal from outside can be delivered into the mitochondrion and converted into the intrinsic execution programme. The other three are respectively the enzyme that cleaves proteins, the fragment produced after bid is cut, and the protein that is released into the cytoplasm to start the intrinsic pathway.

questions.q: After the contractile ring is inhibited, what do these cells become?
options: A cell with two nuclei inside it and a DNA content of 4N.
Programmed cell death: the cell takes itself apart neatly instead of bursting.
The resting branch of the cell cycle, where the cell stays when it is alive but not dividing.
Uncontrolled cell death after injury, in which the contents leak out and cause inflammation in the surrounding tissue.
questions.why: Inhibiting the contractile ring blocks only cytokinesis, and mitosis goes ahead as normal: the chromosomes have replicated and separated but have not been cut into two, so the result is one cell with two nuclei and a DNA content of 4N; on the PI-stained flow cytometry plot you see not two peaks at 2N and 4N but a single 4N peak. This is exactly the first-tier question he named. The other three describe programmed cell death, the G0 resting state and necrosis.

questions.q: In design, how does a bispecific antibody differ from a monospecific antibody?
options: A small membrane bubble that carries cargo from one compartment to the next.
The machine that reads mRNA and joins amino acids one after another.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
An antibody with two different binding heads, which can hit two targets at the same time.
questions.why: A monospecific antibody has a clear limitation: the target must be expressed almost exclusively by the tumour, or normal tissue will be damaged as well. A bispecific antibody puts two binding heads on the same molecule, so it can bind the “tumour-specific antigen” and “another molecule” simultaneously; his example is a tetravalent antibody that hits TRAILR2 and CDH17 together, using a logic gate so that apoptosis is triggered only when both conditions are met. The other three describe the transport vesicle, the ribosome and the lysosome.

questions.q: What is the English name for the concept of “the toxicity a drug causes to the heart”?
options: Apoptosis
cardiotoxicity
Caspase
Cytokinesis
questions.why: cardiotoxicity is exactly the toxicity a drug causes to the heart. Early in drug development, cardiomyocytes induced from iPSCs can be used for in vitro testing, so that cardiotoxicity can be spotted before anyone is dosed; the same logic applies to the liver and the kidney, where human cells are placed into organoids on multiwell plates to run drug screens, reading out activity first and then validating the target. The other three are respectively programmed cell death, the enzyme that cleaves proteins and cytokinesis.

questions.q: What role does the caspase family of enzymes play in apoptosis?
options: The machine that reads mRNA and joins amino acids one after another.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
Enzymes that cut other proteins; the caspase family carries out apoptosis.
The outer skin of the cell. A lipid bilayer that controls what enters and leaves and carries receptors.
questions.why: Caspases are cysteine proteases — the name comes from “cysteine protease”. They normally exist as inactive procaspases; when the time comes, an upstream initiator clips them, exposing a new cleavage site, and then, like a chain reaction, the next caspase is clipped in turn, forming a cascade; the final effector caspases (chiefly caspase 3) shred the cytoskeleton, the nuclear pores and DNA repair proteins, so the cell disassembles into apoptotic bodies. The benefit of this cascade design is that the signal can be amplified. The other three describe the ribosome, the nucleolus and the cell membrane.

questions.q: Using the three-part scheme of “normal liver is safe, normal intestine is safe, colorectal cancer is killed”, why can CDH17 serve as the tumour-targeting end of a bispecific antibody?
options: Normal liver lacks CDH17, and normal intestine expresses CDH17 but is insensitive to TRAIL; only colorectal cancer has both CDH17 and TRAILR2, so only there does the antibody trigger apoptosis.
Uncontrolled cell death after injury, in which the contents leak out and cause inflammation in the surrounding tissue.
The ectoderm. It becomes the skin and the nervous system.
The growth phase of the cell cycle, before DNA replication.
questions.why: CDH17 is a calcium-dependent cell adhesion molecule that is expressed at high level in the intestinal epithelium and at low level in other tissues. The logic of tumour specificity is assembled from three parts: normal liver (CDH17 absent) is safe; normal intestine (CDH17 highly expressed but insensitive to TRAIL) is also safe; colorectal cancer (which has both) is what gets killed. The clinical reality is that cancer cells “throw away” the CDH17 molecule. The other three describe necrosis, the ectoderm and G1 phase.

questions.q: What do drugs of the CDK4/6 inhibitor class do?
options: The resting branch of the cell cycle, where the cell stays when it is alive but not dividing.
The checkpoint in the cell cycle, which only lets the cell proceed once the earlier steps are done.
The cell eats up the parts it does not need, in exchange for nutrients.
It blocks the kinase that lets cells leave G1, so the cell cycle stops; palbociclib is one.
questions.why: For a cell to move from G1 into S phase, Cyclin D must first bind and activate CDK4/6, and the activated CDK4/6 then phosphorylates pRb; once pRb has been phosphorylated it no longer holds E2F, E2F is released, and only then do the S phase genes begin to be transcribed. A CDK4/6 inhibitor blocks that very first gate directly, so the cell stays in G1 — a treatment that “does not kill the cell, only freezes it”. The other three describe the G0 resting state, the checkpoint and autophagy.

questions.q: What is the English name of the timetable made up of G1, S, G2, M and cytokinesis that allows a cell to make a copy of itself?
options: Cell cycle arrest
Cell cycle
M phase
Checkpoint
questions.why: The cell cycle is an ordered timetable: G1 is the growth and preparation phase, S phase replicates the DNA (content going from 2N to 4N), G2 is the check before division, M phase is mitosis, and finally cytokinesis cuts the cytoplasm into two; alongside there is also G0, the resting state that leaves the cycle. What drives this timetable is a switch made of two parts, cyclin (the key) and CDK (the machine). The other three are respectively cell cycle arrest, M phase and the checkpoint.

questions.q: In cell cycle therapy, arrest and killing the cell are two completely different logics; which of the following best captures the nature of arrest?
options: Programmed cell death: the cell takes itself apart neatly instead of bursting.
Uncontrolled cell death after injury, in which the contents leak out and cause inflammation in the surrounding tissue.
The cell stays at a checkpoint, remaining alive but not dividing, so the cell cycle is halted without killing it.
The cell eats up the parts it does not need, in exchange for nutrients.
questions.why: The cell cycle has checkpoints that only let the cell proceed once everything due has been done, and arrest means holding the cell at these gates, alive but not dividing. This is a completely different therapeutic logic from killing the cell: it works on fast-growing tumour cells while affecting normal cells less, and CDK4/6 inhibitors achieve arrest by blocking the gate from G1 to S. Conversely, a tumour that manages to switch off p53, the “final brake”, proliferates more easily. The other three describe programmed cell death, necrosis and autophagy.

questions.q: What is the main function of the centrosome?
options: The organelle that organises microtubules and forms the spindle.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
The power station. It makes most of the ATP, controls apoptosis, and carries its own DNA.
questions.why: The centrosome is the microtubule organising centre of the cell; in mitosis it duplicates into two, moves to opposite poles of the cell and then sends out microtubules from each of them, building the spindle as the “traction scaffold”. It is this structure that allows the spindle fibres to grip the centromere and pull the two sets of sister chromatids towards opposite poles. Cancer cells often have abnormal centrosome numbers, so chromosomes are misallocated and aneuploidy results. The other three describe the nucleolus, the lysosome and the mitochondrion.

questions.q: The cell cycle has gates of the “check first, then carry on” kind: G1/S confirms that the cell is big enough, the DNA is intact and nutrients are plentiful, G2/M confirms that DNA replication is complete, and after M phase there is a further gate confirming that the chromosomes were distributed correctly. What are these gates called?
options: The place where the DNA sits in a bacterial cell, with no membrane around it.
The space between the two mitochondrial membranes, where protons accumulate to drive ATP synthase.
The ectoderm. It becomes the skin and the nervous system.
The checkpoint in the cell cycle, which only lets the cell proceed once the earlier steps are done.
questions.why: The logic of a checkpoint is “check first, then carry on”. The proteins that release or hold the cell (p53, for instance) pause the cycle and start repair when they detect DNA damage; if the damage is too severe to repair, they switch to apoptosis instead. The DDR cascade in the fourth lecture works exactly this way: ATM and ATR sense the damage and the effector p53 decides whether to stop, repair or die. The other three describe the DNA region of a prokaryote, the intermembrane space of the mitochondrion and the ectoderm.

questions.q: What role does the Cip/Kip family play in the cell cycle?
options: The phase of the cell cycle in which the nucleus divides. Mitosis is its first part.
One of the two main families of CDK inhibitors, whose members are p21, p27 and p57.
A protein whose level rises and falls during the cell cycle and switches on the matching CDK; it is the key, not the machine.
The packaging room. It sorts finished proteins and sends them to their destinations.
questions.why: The cell cycle has two braking systems. The Cip/Kip family (p21, p27, p57) is the broad-spectrum one: it binds the whole Cyclin–CDK complex and switches it off entirely; the other family, INK4 (p16/INK4A, p14ARF, p15, p18, p19), targets CDK4/6 alone and is specific. Inhibitory proteins such as p21 and p27 are the cell's own brakes. The other three describe M phase, cyclin and the Golgi apparatus.

questions.q: What is the English name of the end of the Golgi apparatus where vesicles dock and unload (close to the nucleus, facing the ER)?
options: Trans face
Rough ER
Cis face
Smooth ER
questions.why: The cis face is the cis side of the Golgi apparatus, that is, the receiving end: transport vesicles dock here with their cargo, the proteins are processed step by step through the cisternae, and are finally sorted at the trans face and packaged into secretory vesicles for the plasma membrane. Understanding this direction matters: secretory proteins come in at the cis face and go out at the trans face. The other three are respectively the shipping end and the two regions of the endoplasmic reticulum.

questions.q: What structures are the cisternae inside the Golgi apparatus, and what role do they play?
options: Flattened sac-like structures stacked in layers inside the Golgi apparatus.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
The space between the two mitochondrial membranes, where protons accumulate to drive ATP synthase.
questions.why: The cisternae are the flattened sac-like structures stacked in layers inside the Golgi apparatus, like the stations of a production line: after entering at the cis face, proteins are processed and sorted as they pass layer by layer through the cisternae, with transport vesicles relaying between one layer and the next, the direction running from the cis face towards the trans face and being irreversible, until the proteins are packaged into secretory vesicles and sent to the plasma membrane. The other three describe the nucleolus, the lysosome and the intermembrane space of the mitochondrion.

questions.q: After the contractile ring is inhibited, what happens respectively to the distribution of the chromosomes and to the division of the cell itself?
options: The phase of the cell cycle in which the nucleus divides. Mitosis is its first part.
The step that splits the cytoplasm into two after mitosis.
The cell eats up the parts it does not need, in exchange for nutrients.
The chromosomes separate perfectly normally, but the contractile ring does not tighten, so the cytoplasm is never cut in two; the result is one cell with two nuclei and a DNA content of 4N.
questions.why: The machine that cuts the cytoplasm apart is the contractile ring: bundles of actin filaments are pulled by myosin, tightening like elastic bands from the centre of the cell until a cleavage furrow forms and divides the cell in two. When the contractile ring is inhibited (by a drug or by knocking down its expression), the chromosomes still separate normally but the cell cannot divide, giving one cell with two nuclei and a DNA content of 4N; he says he asks this question every time, and that only half the students got it right last year. The other three describe M phase, cytokinesis and autophagy.

questions.q: Which part of the mitochondrion are the cristae, and what is their function?
options: The liquid interior of the mitochondrion, where the TCA cycle runs and mitochondrial DNA also lies.
The folds that the inner mitochondrial membrane makes inwards, on which the ATP-making machinery sits.
The space between the two mitochondrial membranes, where protons accumulate to drive ATP synthase.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
questions.why: The cristae are folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane that multiply its surface area many times over; both the electron transport chain and ATP synthase need a large membrane area to work, so the denser the folds, the more ATP can be made, and oxidative phosphorylation takes place precisely here. A normal aerobic cell earns about 36 ATP per glucose, whereas a cancer cell relying on aerobic glycolysis earns only about 4. The other three describe the mitochondrial matrix, the intermembrane space and the nucleolus.

questions.q: At meiosis I, what is the English name of the process in which DNA is deliberately exchanged between homologous chromosomes, reshuffling genetic variation?
options: mitotic recombination
recombinant chromatids
Crossing over
Meiosis
questions.why: Crossing over takes place in meiosis I, when homologous chromosomes pair up, and the site of the exchange is called a chiasma; after the exchange one chromosome carries a segment from the maternal side and a segment from the paternal side, so that every gamete produced differs from the parents and from its siblings. The fourth lecture stresses that all of this uses the very same homologous recombination machinery that normally repairs DNA, deliberately borrowed in meiosis to rearrange genes. The other three are respectively the exchange that occurs during mitosis, the chromatids carrying new combinations after the crossover, and the whole process of meiosis.

questions.q: The switch of the cell cycle has two parts: the CDK is the machine standing on standby, while the other part, whose concentration rises and falls with the cycle, is responsible for lighting up the matching CDK. This part is called ______.
options: A protein whose level rises and falls during the cell cycle and switches on the matching CDK; it is the key, not the machine.
The phase of the cell cycle in which the nucleus divides. Mitosis is its first part.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
questions.why: The CDK is the machine that does the real work, but it stands on standby and has to be switched on by a cyclin: the concentration of the cyclin rises and falls with the cycle, and a particular cyclin is made in bulk at a particular moment so that it partners with its CDK, lights that CDK up and drives that step forward; afterwards the cyclin is degraded and the CDK switches off again, which is why the name “cycle” comes from the cyclin and not from the cycle itself. The clinical relevance appears in drug therapy: a CDK4/6 inhibitor blocks the Cyclin D–CDK4/6 step, so the cell stays in G1. The other three describe M phase, the lysosome and the nucleolus.

questions.q: What kind of enzyme is a cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK)?
options: A protein whose level rises and falls during the cell cycle and switches on the matching CDK; it is the key, not the machine.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
The packaging room. It sorts finished proteins and sends them to their destinations.
An enzyme that drives one step of the cell cycle; it works only when switched on by its matching cyclin.
questions.why: A CDK is a serine/threonine kinase, and its activity needs two conditions: that it is bound by a cyclin, and that another subunit is phosphorylated. It is not a machine that repeats the same job; it is switched on by the cyclin again and again, does one step and is then switched off, and its output is phosphorylation — for instance Cyclin D–CDK4/6 phosphorylates pRb, and once pRb lets go, E2F is released and the genes needed for S phase begin to be transcribed. The other three describe cyclin, the lysosome and the Golgi apparatus.

questions.q: Apart from its day job of carrying electrons, what is the second job of cytochrome c?
options: A protein whose level rises and falls during the cell cycle and switches on the matching CDK; it is the key, not the machine.
A protein that normally sits in the mitochondrion and, once released into the cytoplasm, starts the intrinsic apoptosis pathway.
The machine that reads mRNA and joins amino acids one after another.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
questions.why: The day job of cytochrome c is as one link in the electron transport chain, shuttling electrons between the inner mitochondrial membrane and complex III; but it has a second job as well: in the intrinsic apoptosis pathway it acts as the switch. When the pro-apoptotic members of the Bcl-2 family, bak and bax, puncture the outer mitochondrial membrane, cytochrome c leaks into the cytoplasm, binds APAF-1, assembles the apoptosome and activates caspase 9. The other three describe cyclin, the ribosome and the lysosome.

questions.q: What is the last step of the cell cycle, “splitting the cytoplasm in two”, and how is the division of labour with mitosis?
options: The division of the nucleus, in which the replicated chromosomes separate.
The phase of the cell cycle in which the nucleus divides. Mitosis is its first part.

Cytokinesis cuts the cytoplasm apart with a contractile ring made of actin and myosin (plant cells instead grow a cell plate), and it is a mutually independent event from mitosis, in which the chromosomes are separated; the two also run to different timetables.
The part of mitosis in which the chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles.
questions.why: When the contractile ring is inhibited the chromosomes separate perfectly well but the cell cannot be cut open, so the result is a binucleated cell with one cell, two nuclei and a DNA content of 4N; a further detail is that organelles are distributed at random, so the severity of a mitochondrial disease can differ greatly between siblings. The other three describe mitosis, M phase and anaphase.

questions.q: The cytoskeleton is made of three kinds of fibre — actin microfilaments, intermediate filaments and tubulin microtubules; which of the following best summarises its overall role?
options: The network of fibres that gives the cell its shape, moves cargo, forms the spindle and pinches the cell in two.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
The power station. It makes most of the ATP, controls apoptosis, and carries its own DNA.
questions.why: Actin governs shape and movement and is also a component of the contractile ring; microtubules are the tracks for long-distance transport and also the scaffold of the spindle during division; intermediate filaments mainly give the cell mechanical strength. Clinically there are three immediate consequences: blocking the contractile ring produces binucleated cells; microtubule drugs disturb the spindle so that chromosomes cannot be allocated correctly; and the migration and invasion of cancer cells depend on laying down new actin networks. The other three describe the nucleolus, the lysosome and the mitochondrion.

questions.q: What is the English name for the concept of “a receptor on the cell surface that starts apoptosis as soon as an external signal touches it”?
options: Caspase
Apoptosome
TRAIL
Death receptor
questions.why: The death receptor is the entry point of the extrinsic apoptosis pathway and belongs to the TNF receptor superfamily, the most typical example being DR5 (the receptor for TRAIL). When the ligand binds, trimerisation of the receptor brings the intracellular death domains together, recruiting and activating caspase 8, which then cleaves procaspase 3 and apoptosis is under way; sometimes it also cleaves bid to produce tbid and carries the signal into the mitochondrion. The other three are respectively the enzyme that cleaves proteins, the wheel-shaped apoptotic complex and the extrinsic ligand that starts apoptosis.

questions.q: What is the English name of the process by which cells carrying the same DNA switch on different sets of genes, make different proteins and fold into different shapes?
options: Pluripotent
Differentiation
Multipotent
Yamanaka factors
questions.why: A fertilised egg divides to give rise to nerve cells, muscle cells and liver cells, each carrying the same DNA yet doing different work; what sends them down different paths is differentiation. In the second lecture he turns this into a reversible experiment in the iPSC section, using Yamanaka factors to reprogramme fibroblasts into a pluripotent state and then differentiating them into cardiomyocytes or neurons. The other three are respectively the potency that can become almost any cell type, the potency that can become several cell types of one family, and the four reprogramming factors.

questions.q: In G1 phase pRb holds a certain transcription factor so that the S phase genes are not switched on; when the cyclin D–CDK4/6 complex phosphorylates pRb, this transcription factor is released. What is this transcription factor called?
options: The resting branch of the cell cycle, where the cell stays when it is alive but not dividing.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
A transcription factor normally held down by pRb; it is released when the cell is ready to divide.
The protein that holds the cell cycle in G1 until the cell is ready to replicate its DNA.
questions.why: E2F is a group of transcription factors that control the genes needed to enter S phase, such as the enzymes of DNA replication; the cell's gate is pRb, which in G1 binds E2F and holds it down so that the S phase genes are not switched on, and once cyclin D–CDK4/6 phosphorylates pRb, E2F is released and the whole battery of S phase genes is switched on. This is also why CDK4/6 inhibitors such as palbociclib work: weld the gate shut and the cell stays in G1. The other three describe G0, the lysosome and pRb.

questions.q: What is the English name of the outermost of the three germ layers of the embryo, which becomes the skin and the nervous system?
options: Ectoderm
Endoderm
Mesoderm
Yamanaka factors
questions.why: The ectoderm becomes skin and hair, the nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the epithelium of the sensory organs; in the validation of iPSCs the three layers are the gold standard: only if iPSCs injected into an immunodeficient mouse grow into a teratoma containing tissue from all three germ layers is it proved that they really are pluripotent. The other three are respectively the endoderm, which becomes the gut lining and the lung, the mesoderm, which becomes muscle, bone and blood, and the four factors used for reprogramming.

questions.q: Into which tissues does the endoderm differentiate?
options: The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
The power station. It makes most of the ATP, controls apoptosis, and carries its own DNA.
The outer skin of the cell. A lipid bilayer that controls what enters and leaves and carries receptors.
The endoderm. It becomes the gut lining and the lung.
questions.why: The endoderm is the innermost of the three germ layers; it forms the epithelium of the digestive tract (the gut lining), the epithelium of the lung and the trachea, the parenchyma of the liver and pancreas, and the epithelium of the bladder. Its significance lies in the fact that “the same genome, completely different fates in different germ layers”, which is the framework for understanding cell fate determination and the differentiation capacity of iPSCs. The other three describe the nucleolus, the mitochondrion and the outer skin of the cell.

questions.q: What does the concept of endosymbiotic origin mean?
options: Only one set of chromosomes, as gametes are. Human gametes have 23.
The idea that mitochondria were originally bacteria, swallowed up by an ancestral cell and kept.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
The outer skin of the cell. A lipid bilayer that controls what enters and leaves and carries receptors.
questions.why: The plausible explanation runs like this: in the distant past some prokaryotic cell took in an aerobic bacterium without digesting it, the two lived together in symbiosis for a long time, the one that was swallowed kept its capacity for respiratory metabolism and the host gained an extra power station. Mitochondria have their own DNA (about 17 kb and 37 genes) and their own ribosomes, and they have a double membrane with the inner one folded into cristae and the outer one more like a bacterial membrane, all of which supports this explanation; it leaves three verifiable consequences: the maternal inheritance of mtDNA, and the fact that mitochondrial disease can be explained by the threshold effect. The other three describe haploidy, the nucleolus and the cell membrane.

questions.q: What is the definition of a eukaryotic cell, and what regulatory advantage does it bring?
options: Cells with no nucleus. Bacteria and archaea are all prokaryotes.
The place where the DNA sits in a bacterial cell, with no membrane around it.
Cells with a nucleus. Animals, plants, fungi and yeast are all eukaryotes.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
questions.why: The dividing line between eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells is a membrane-bound nucleus. With a nucleus, the DNA is shut in the control room and transcription and translation take place in different places with RNA processing (splicing, capping, poly-A tailing) in between; this two-stage arrangement is precisely what makes alternative splicing and fine regulation possible. Prokaryotes have no nucleus, so replication and production happen in the same place at the same time, quick and simple, but for the same reason they lack the machinery for folding and modifying complex proteins. The other three describe prokaryotic cells, the DNA region of a prokaryote and the lysosome.

questions.q: What is the English name of the apoptosis pathway started by an extracellular ligand binding a receptor on the cell surface, and started via caspase-8?
options: Extrinsic apoptosis pathway
Intrinsic apoptosis pathway
Apoptosis
Autophagy
questions.why: This pathway begins outside the cell: a ligand such as TRAIL binds a death receptor such as DR5, and the intracellular part of the receptor immediately recruits procaspase-8 to start the caspase cascade; caspase-8 on the one hand cleaves procaspase-3 and on the other cleaves bid to produce tbid, carrying the signal into the mitochondrion so that the intrinsic pathway is started as well. His clinical example is the bispecific antibody BI 905711, which recognises TRAILR2 and CDH17 at the same time and induces apoptosis only when both are present. The other three are respectively the intrinsic pathway started by the mitochondrion, programmed cell death and autophagy.

questions.q: What does fetal bovine serum (FBS) provide in cell culture?
options: The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
The packaging room. It sorts finished proteins and sends them to their destinations.
The bovine serum used to grow cells, which supplies growth factors.
questions.why: FBS is the liquid part of calf blood, and it contains the factors that let cells grow and divide; cell culture commonly uses 10% FBS, but for cell cycle synchronisation it is cut to 0.5–1%, so that the cells stop in G1 for lack of growth factors. Because the composition varies with the state of the cow, rigorous experiments fix on one batch of serum and record its batch number, or the data will carry a systematic bias. The other three describe the lysosome, the nucleolus and the Golgi apparatus.

questions.q: On the cell cycle diagram there is a side branch running off from G1, where the cell is alive and metabolically normal but no longer replicates DNA and no longer divides; cells that are highly differentiated (neurons and muscle cells, for example) stay here permanently. This branch is called ______.
options: The growth phase of the cell cycle, before DNA replication.
The resting branch of the cell cycle, where the cell stays when it is alive but not dividing.
The checkpoint phase after DNA replication is complete and before the cell divides.
The part of the cell cycle in which DNA is replicated.
questions.why: G0 is a side branch running off G1 on the cell cycle diagram; cells that enter G0 are alive and metabolically normal but no longer replicate DNA and no longer divide, while stem cells can return to G1 as needed. Clinically G0 has two uses: serum starvation is used to hold cultured cells in G1 and release them synchronously, which is standard practice for studying DNA replication; and “cellular quiescence” is not the same as “cell death”, so a halted cycle does not mean apoptosis. The other three describe G1, G2 and S phase.

questions.q: Why do cells treated with a CDK4/6 inhibitor such as palbociclib stay in G1, with DNA content held at 2N?
options: The checkpoint phase after DNA replication is complete and before the cell divides.
The part of the cell cycle in which DNA is replicated.
Because the gate from G1 to S is pRb–E2F: with cyclin D–CDK4/6 blocked, pRb is not phosphorylated, E2F stays held down, the S phase genes cannot be switched on, and the cell remains in G1.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
questions.why: G1 is the phase in which the cell “grows”; the DNA has not yet been replicated, so the DNA content is 2N, and after PI staining this is the leftmost 2N peak on the flow cytometry plot. There are two gates at the exit from G1: one is pRb–E2F and the other is the DNA damage checkpoint, and CDK4/6 inhibitors jam the first of these gates. The other three describe G2, S phase and the lysosome.

questions.q: The phase in which DNA replication is complete (DNA content 4N) but the cell has not yet divided, whose job is to “check the copy”; if the check fails the cell stays here, if it cannot be repaired it heads towards apoptosis, and only if the check passes does it enter M phase. This phase is called ______.
options: The checkpoint phase after DNA replication is complete and before the cell divides.
The growth phase of the cell cycle, before DNA replication.
The part of the cell cycle in which DNA is replicated.
The resting branch of the cell cycle, where the cell stays when it is alive but not dividing.
questions.why: G2 is the phase in which DNA replication is complete but the cell has not yet divided, and its job is to “check the copy”; if the check fails, the cell stays here, and if the damage cannot be repaired it heads towards apoptosis, while only a passed check allows entry into M phase. The G2/M junction is the most important gate of the cell cycle, which is why many anticancer drugs target this point. The other three describe G1, S phase and G0.

questions.q: What role does the Golgi apparatus play in the secretory pathway?
options: The part of the endoplasmic reticulum that carries ribosomes, where new proteins are made and folded.
The part of the endoplasmic reticulum with no ribosomes attached, which makes lipids.
The machine that reads mRNA and joins amino acids one after another.
The packaging room. It sorts finished proteins and sends them to their destinations.
questions.why: The Golgi apparatus is a stack of flattened sacs downstream of the ER: transport vesicles coming from the ER first fuse with the cis face (the receiving face), the proteins are modified and sorted layer by layer, and they then leave from the trans face (the shipping face), are packaged into secretory vesicles and, on fusion with the plasma membrane, are delivered to the cell surface or released outside the cell. The same protein passing through the Golgi may acquire different modifying groups and so be sorted to different destinations, which is the working logic of “sorting and delivery”. The other three describe the rough ER, the smooth ER and the ribosome.

questions.q: What is the English name for the state of “having only one set of chromosomes” (human gametes have 23)?
options: Pluripotent
Haploid
Multipotent
Homoplasmy
questions.why: Haploid (n) means one set of chromosomes: each human gamete has 23 chromosomes (22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome), and after fertilisation it fuses with another gamete to become diploid (2n = 46). Meiosis is a “machine of diversity” because the first division separates the homologous chromosomes and the second separates the sister chromatids; non-disjunction can also produce nullisomic or disomic gametes, which after fertilisation give rise to monosomy (2n−1) or trisomy (2n+1). The other three are respectively the potency that can become almost any cell type, the potency that can become several cell types of one family, and the state of mitochondrial DNA.

questions.q: What is the medical significance of the state in which normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA are mixed together inside the same cell?
options: Every copy of mitochondrial DNA in a cell is identical, whether normal or mutant.
Disease appears only when the proportion of mutant mitochondrial DNA exceeds a particular tissue's tolerance limit.

Whether disease appears depends on whether the proportion of mutant mtDNA passes the threshold for that tissue: skeletal muscle, which has high energy demand, has a low threshold and is affected first, whereas hearing has a high threshold and is affected later.
The rule that mitochondrial disease is passed from an affected mother to all her children, and from an affected father to none.
questions.why: Every mitochondrion carries its own copy of DNA, so normal and mutant mtDNA can exist side by side inside one cell; this mixed state is called heteroplasmy. Carrying mutant mtDNA does not mean you will fall ill: symptoms appear only once the proportion of mutant mtDNA exceeds the tolerance limit of a particular tissue. Clinically the proportion of mtDNA is estimated from a muscle biopsy or from blood, but note that the threshold in blood differs from that in muscle. The other three describe the state in which everything is identical, the threshold effect itself, and maternal inheritance.

questions.q: What is the English name for the state in which every copy of mitochondrial DNA in a cell is identical, whether normal or mutant?
options: Homoplasmy
Heteroplasmy
Threshold effect
Mitochondrial Eve
questions.why: Homoplasmy is the counterpart of heteroplasmy: all copies of mtDNA in a cell are identical, either all normal (healthy homoplasmy) or all mutant (mutant homoplasmy). Disease mostly appears in the heteroplasmic state in between, and only once the proportion of mutant mtDNA passes the threshold of that tissue, so the severity can differ greatly between tissues in the same patient. The other three are respectively the mixing of normal and mutant, the threshold effect and Mitochondrial Eve.

questions.q: What is the English name of the family of proteins that binds caspase-9 and caspase-3 directly and holds the executioners of apoptosis?
options: Caspase
Apoptosome
Bcl-2 family
Inhibitor of apoptosis (IAP)
questions.why: IAP stands for inhibitor of apoptosis; structurally it contains repeated BIR domains, which allow it to bind caspase-9 and caspase-3 directly, hold the executioners and put the “brake” on the apoptotic signal. In normal cells, IAP and mechanisms such as XIAP ensure that only cells that really should die are cleared away; tumours often escape apoptosis by overexpressing IAP (survivin, for instance), which makes IAP inhibitors an active direction in anticancer drug development. The other three are respectively the enzyme that cleaves proteins, the wheel-shaped apoptotic complex and the family that decides whether the mitochondrion releases the apoptotic signal.

questions.q: How do the inhibitory proteins of the INK4 family work?
options: The resting branch of the cell cycle, where the cell stays when it is alive but not dividing.
A family of inhibitory proteins that block CDK4/6 kinase and so stop the cell cycle.
Programmed cell death: the cell takes itself apart neatly instead of bursting.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
questions.why: INK4 stands for Inhibitor of CDK4 and is a family of CKIs, including p16INK4A, p15INK4B, p18INK4C and p19INK4D. They bind CDK4 or CDK6 and stop it, so that pRb is not phosphorylated, E2F is not released, and the cell stays in G1, unable to enter S phase. The most clinically relevant is mutation or promoter methylation of CDKN2A (p16INK4A); alongside the INK4 family there is another group, Cip/Kip (p21, p27, p57). The other three describe G0, programmed cell death and the nucleolus.

questions.q: A mitochondrion has an outer and an inner membrane, and in the space between them protons are pumped to a high concentration, and the gradient that forms drives ATP synthase to make ATP. This space is called ______.
options: The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
The liquid interior of the mitochondrion, where the TCA cycle runs and mitochondrial DNA also lies.
The space between the two mitochondrial membranes, where protons accumulate to drive ATP synthase.
The outer skin of the cell. A lipid bilayer that controls what enters and leaves and carries receptors.
questions.why: As electrons pass along the respiratory chain from complexes I, III and IV, protons are pumped from the matrix into the intermembrane space, so the proton concentration there is far higher than in the matrix and an electrochemical gradient forms; the protons then flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase, converting that gradient energy into ATP. The inner membrane is highly impermeable to ions, which is what holds the gradient in place, whereas the outer membrane is comparatively permeable, like a sieve; the intermembrane space is small in volume, so the proton concentration can be driven very high. The other three describe the nucleolus, the mitochondrial matrix and the cell membrane.

questions.q: What is the English name of the apoptosis pathway driven by internal stress (DNA damage, hypoxia, lack of growth factors), which acts on the Bcl-2 family and starts through the release of cytochrome c from the mitochondrion?
options: Intrinsic apoptosis pathway
Extrinsic apoptosis pathway
Apoptosome
Autophagy
questions.why: This pathway is started by internal stress signals; when bak and bax gain the upper hand, cytochrome c is released from the intermembrane space into the cytoplasm, joins APAF-1 and procaspase-9 to form the apoptosome, activates caspase-9, which then cleaves procaspase-3 into the executioner caspase-3, and the cell is dismantled in an orderly way; if bcl-2 gains the upper hand instead, the mitochondrion seals cytochrome c in and the cell survives — which is where the idea of “the mitochondrion as the control centre of cell death” comes from. The other three are respectively the extrinsic pathway, the wheel-shaped complex and autophagy.

questions.q: What is an iPSC, and how does it differ from an ordinary adult cell?
options: The place where the DNA sits in a bacterial cell, with no membrane around it.
Cells with no nucleus. Bacteria and archaea are all prokaryotes.
The power station. It makes most of the ATP, controls apoptosis, and carries its own DNA.
An adult cell reprogrammed back to an embryo-like state, so that it can become almost any cell type.
questions.why: An iPSC is the product of reprogramming a mature somatic cell (a fibroblast, for instance) back to a pluripotent state using the four Yamanaka factors (Oct3/4, Sox2, c-Myc, Klf4), and it can therefore become almost any cell type. The advantage is that it sidesteps the ethical controversy around embryonic stem cells, and because it uses the patient's own cells it should in principle be possible to make immunocompatible cells for transplantation. Validation takes three layers: morphology, markers (surface marker, PCR, flow cytometry), and the gold-standard teratoma assay. The other three describe the DNA region of bacteria, prokaryotic cells and the mitochondrion.

questions.q: What is the English name for the recycling plant inside the cell that has an acidic interior, is loaded with digestive enzymes and breaks down foreign material and damaged organelles into amino acids and monosaccharides?
options: The packaging room. It sorts finished proteins and sends them to their destinations.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
The control room. It keeps the DNA and decides which genes are read.
The power station. It makes most of the ATP, controls apoptosis, and carries its own DNA.
questions.why: The lysosome is a vesicle enclosed by a single membrane whose interior is acidic and which is loaded with digestive enzymes; its job is to break down engulfed foreign material, damaged organelles (autophagy) and worn-out proteins into amino acids and monosaccharides and return them to the cytoplasm for reuse. The acidity of the lysosome is maintained by proton pumps in the membrane, and the digestive enzymes are only active in this acidic environment. The other three are respectively the packaging and sorting room, the control room and the mitochondrion.

questions.q: What is the relationship between M phase and the G2/M peak on a flow cytometry plot?
options: The part of the cell cycle in which DNA is replicated.
The growth phase of the cell cycle, before DNA replication.
M phase comprises mitosis and cytokinesis, and cells in G2 and in M both have a DNA content of 4N, so flow cytometry can only lump them together into a single G2/M peak.
The part of mitosis in which the chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles.
questions.why: M phase comprises mitosis (separation of the chromosomes) and cytokinesis (division of the cytoplasm), and he stresses that the two are mutually independent: inhibiting the contractile ring only turns the cell into a binucleated one, while the chromosomes still separate normally. Chromosome separation is driven by the spindle fibres, whereas the contractile ring is responsible only for cutting the cytoplasm in two, and the two processes are controlled by different proteins. The other three describe S phase, G1 and anaphase.

questions.q: What rule about mitochondrial disease does maternal inheritance express?
options: The rule that mitochondrial disease is passed from an affected mother to all her children, and from an affected father to none.
On the father's side.
The proportion of people carrying the mutation who actually develop disease. It is never 100%.
Disease appears only when the proportion of mutant mitochondrial DNA exceeds a particular tissue's tolerance limit.
questions.why: The mitochondria brought in by the sperm are destroyed after fertilisation, so mtDNA travels almost exclusively down the maternal line; the features by which it is recognised are that an affected mother passes the disease to all her children, an affected father passes it to none, and the disease appears in every generation. Clinically the threshold effect must also be taken into account: disease appears only when the proportion of mutant mtDNA exceeds the tolerance of the tissue in question, with the high energy demand of skeletal muscle giving a low threshold and so being affected first, and hearing having a high threshold and being affected later. One turning point to keep in mind is that mitochondrial disease can also arise from mutations in nuclear genes, in which case the inheritance pattern is Mendelian. The other three are the paternal side, penetrance and the threshold effect.

questions.q: What mainly takes place in the matrix of the mitochondrion?
options: The space between the two mitochondrial membranes, where protons accumulate to drive ATP synthase.
The folds that the inner mitochondrial membrane makes inwards, on which the ATP-making machinery sits.
The power station. It makes most of the ATP, controls apoptosis, and carries its own DNA.
The liquid interior of the mitochondrion, where the TCA cycle runs and mitochondrial DNA also lies.
questions.why: The matrix is the liquid space enclosed by the inner membrane; the TCA cycle runs there, oxidising the carbons of acetyl-CoA step by step into carbon dioxide and storing the released electrons in NADH and FADH₂; it also houses that circle of about 17 kb of mtDNA and the mitochondrion's own ribosome, and is almost completely isolated from the metabolism of the cytoplasm. The other three describe the intermembrane space, the cristae formed by folds of the inner membrane, and the mitochondrion as a whole.

questions.q: What is the English name of the special division that produces four genetically different gametes and separates the homologous chromosomes and the sister chromatids in two rounds?
options: Mitosis
Meiosis
Crossing over
recombinant chromatids
questions.why: Compared with mitosis, meiosis does two things: the first division separates the homologous chromosomes and the second separates the sister chromatids, so one diploid starting cell produces four haploid gametes; in between there is a crossover that reshuffles the alleles. With random segregation and random fertilisation on top, genetic diversity is almost unlimited. The other three are respectively ordinary mitosis in which chromosomes separate, the crossover step within meiosis, and the chromatids produced after the crossover.

questions.q: Into which tissues does the mesoderm differentiate?
options: The endoderm. It becomes the gut lining and the lung.
The ectoderm. It becomes the skin and the nervous system.
The mesoderm. It becomes muscle, bone and blood.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
questions.why: Of the three germ layers the mesoderm comes in the middle, and it produces tissues including muscle, bone, cartilage, blood and most of the cells of the lymphoid system, as well as the kidney and the reproductive system. The significance of the layers is experimental: if iPSCs injected into an immunodeficient mouse form a teratoma in which tissue from all three germ layers is found at the same time, this proves that the cells really are pluripotent. The other three describe the endoderm, the ectoderm and the nucleolus.

questions.q: What role does the microtubule play in the cell?
options: A hollow tube made of protein, which forms the mitotic spindle and also serves as a track for cargo.
The motor protein that builds the contractile ring together with actin.
The folds that the inner mitochondrial membrane makes inwards, on which the ATP-making machinery sits.
The cell eats up the parts it does not need, in exchange for nutrients.
questions.why: Microtubules are built from tubulin and are hollow tubes, with a GTP end at one side and a GDP end at the other, assembling and disassembling continuously inside the cell. The microtubules of the spindle grip the centromere of the chromosomes and pull the sister chromatids towards opposite poles; at the same time they are the tracks for organelle transport, with kinesin and dynein dragging cargo across the cell along them. The other three describe the motor protein of the contractile ring, the folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane and autophagy.

questions.q: What are the characteristics of the shape, size and inheritance of mitochondrial DNA?
options: The double membrane that encloses the nucleus.
The place where the DNA sits in a bacterial cell, with no membrane around it.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
The small circular DNA inside the mitochondrion, about 17 kilobases and carrying 37 genes. It is inherited from the mother.
questions.why: mtDNA is a circle of double-stranded circular DNA, about 17 kb, carrying 37 genes (mostly tRNAs and components of the respiratory chain), and it encodes its own rRNA and tRNA. What makes it special is that it is handed down single-lineage from the mother and that every cell has many copies, so normal and mutant mtDNA can exist side by side in one person, which is heteroplasmy. The other three describe the nuclear envelope, the DNA region of a prokaryotic cell and the nucleolus.

questions.q: Why can it be said that all the mitochondrial DNA still present in living humans descends from one woman?
options: Only one set of chromosomes, as gametes are. Human gametes have 23.

Because mtDNA travels almost exclusively down the maternal line, all the mtDNA now present in humans can be traced back to the same maternal lineage, and mitochondrial DNA went through a “bottleneck” that left only a few women.
On the father's side.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
questions.why: All the mtDNA now present in humans can be traced back to the same maternal lineage, and mitochondrial DNA passed through a “bottleneck” between several thousand and several tens of thousands of years ago, leaving only a few women, after which no mtDNA from any other source is seen again. Her existence is inferred from the differences in mtDNA, not from an individual found in the fossil record; his slides also mention that rare cases of paternal mtDNA transmission do indeed exist. The other three describe haploidy, the father's side and the nucleolus.

questions.q: What are the three identities of the mitochondrion?
options: The space between the two mitochondrial membranes, where protons accumulate to drive ATP synthase.
The liquid interior of the mitochondrion, where the TCA cycle runs and mitochondrial DNA also lies.
The power station. It makes most of the ATP, controls apoptosis, and carries its own DNA.
The folds that the inner mitochondrial membrane makes inwards, on which the ATP-making machinery sits.
questions.why: The three identities fit together: ATP synthase on the inner membrane generates electricity from the proton gradient; when the cell has to dispose of itself the mitochondrion releases cytochrome c, triggering the apoptosome and caspase 9; and it carries its own circular DNA and ribosome. Its origin is endosymbiotic: an ancestral eukaryotic cell swallowed a bacterium and the two went on living together. The other three describe the intermembrane space, the matrix and the folds of the inner membrane.

questions.q: What does mitosis cover?
options: The division of the nucleus, in which the replicated chromosomes separate.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
The outer skin of the cell. A lipid bilayer that controls what enters and leaves and carries receptors.
questions.why: Mitosis touches only the chromosomes and the nucleus: in prophase the chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes and the spindle forms, in metaphase the chromosomes line up on the equatorial plate, in anaphase the sister chromatids are pulled towards opposite poles, and in telophase the nuclear envelope is rebuilt. Whether the cytoplasm divides is another matter; the two events are independent, which is why the questions he sets can be taken apart cleanly. The other three describe the nucleolus, the lysosome and the cell membrane.

questions.q: When the repeat regions of pericentromeric heterochromatin lose their methylation, the cell may exchange material between the repeats during mitosis, so the chromosomes are reallocated and duplications and deletions appear, which is one source of genomic instability and CNV. This process is called ______.
options: The part of mitosis in which the chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles.
Chromatids carrying new combinations after the crossover.
The deliberate exchange of DNA between homologous chromosomes in meiosis, which reshuffles genetic variation.
Chromosomal crossover occurring during mitosis.
questions.why: Mitotic recombination is the chromosomal crossover that occurs during mitosis: when the repeat regions lose their methylation (are hypomethylated), the cell may exchange material between the repeats during mitosis, the chromosomes are reallocated and duplications and deletions appear, which is one source of genomic instability and one of the mechanisms by which CNVs are generated. The other three describe anaphase, the chromatids after the crossover and the crossover in meiosis.

questions.q: What is the mitotic spindle made of, and what does it do?
options: A hollow tube made of protein, which forms the mitotic spindle and also serves as a track for cargo.
A rope made of microtubules that pulls the replicated chromosomes apart.
The organelle that organises microtubules and forms the spindle.
The control room. It keeps the DNA and decides which genes are read.
questions.why: The spindle is built from microtubules and associated proteins; in metaphase it lines the centromeres of the chromosomes up on the equatorial plate, and in anaphase it uses the shortening of the microtubules to send the sister chromatids towards opposite poles. Its assembly and disassembly are dynamic, and for chromosomes to be distributed correctly into two daughter cells this machine has to hold the sister chromatids in the right position. The other three describe microtubules, the organising centre of the spindle and the nucleus.

questions.q: What situation produces a multinucleated cell?
options: Programmed cell death: the cell takes itself apart neatly instead of bursting.
The cell eats up the parts it does not need, in exchange for nutrients.
A cell with more than one nucleus, because the cytoplasm did not divide.
Uncontrolled cell death after injury, in which the contents leak out and cause inflammation in the surrounding tissue.
questions.why: When the contractile ring (the ring of actin and myosin) is inhibited, mitosis goes ahead normally and the chromosomes still separate, but the cell cannot be cut into two daughter cells; the result is a cell with two or more nuclei and a DNA content of 4N, and flow cytometry shows a single 4N peak rather than separate 2N and 4N peaks. There are two ways to destroy the contractile ring: suppress the expression of its proteins, or apply an inhibitor directly. The other three describe programmed cell death, autophagy and necrosis.

questions.q: What is the definition of multipotent?
options: Cells that can become several cell types, but only within the same family.
The ectoderm. It becomes the skin and the nervous system.
The mesoderm. It becomes muscle, bone and blood.
The endoderm. It becomes the gut lining and the lung.
questions.why: Multipotency is lower than pluripotency. The haematopoietic stem cell is the typical case: it can become red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets, but not neurons or skin cells. Adult stem cells have limited self-renewal and usually divide only a limited number of times, whereas ESCs and iPSCs are pluripotent and can differentiate into almost every somatic cell type, yet still cannot form a whole individual. The other three describe the three germ layers.

questions.q: What is the English name of the protein whose head is a motor that walks along actin fibres using ATP and pulls the filaments towards itself?
options: Actin
Caspase
Ribosome
Myosin
questions.why: The head of myosin is a motor that “walks” along actin fibres step by step, consuming ATP and pulling the filaments towards itself; a dividing cell assembles an actin–myosin contractile ring near the equatorial plate, and the tightening of that ring produces a groove that pinches the cell into two. When the contractile ring is inhibited all you see is a binucleated cell, while the chromosomes still separate normally, which is exactly the evidence he uses to stress that mitosis and cytokinesis are mutually independent. The other three are respectively actin, the enzyme that cleaves proteins and the ribosome.

questions.q: In the tumour microenvironment, what chain of events does necrosis trigger?
options: Programmed cell death: the cell takes itself apart neatly instead of bursting.
Necrosis causes local hypoxia and acidification, and hypoxia is precisely the signal for HIF-1α to accumulate, which then drives the adaptation and progression of the tumour.
The cell eats up the parts it does not need, in exchange for nutrients.
The cell designating itself as one particular specialised cell type.
questions.why: Necrosis is not a programmed death: the plasma membrane breaks down first, the contents leak out and an inflammatory reaction is triggered; apoptosis, by contrast, is the cell tidying up after itself, with the membrane intact and the contents packaged into apoptotic bodies that are swallowed up, so very little inflammation results. In a tumour, necrosis often causes hypoxia and acidification, and hypoxia is precisely the signal for HIF-1α to accumulate. The other three describe programmed cell death, autophagy and differentiation.

questions.q: The structure of two membranes that encloses the RNA and DNA, is linked in between by the nuclear pore complex, and is continuous with the outer membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum is called ______.
options: The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
The outer skin of the cell. A lipid bilayer that controls what enters and leaves and carries receptors.
The double membrane that encloses the nucleus.
The place where the DNA sits in a bacterial cell, with no membrane around it.
questions.why: The nuclear envelope is two membranes enclosing the RNA and DNA, joined in between by the nuclear pore complex; it separates transcription from translation, so a eukaryotic cell has to process and vet the pre-mRNA before sending it out of the nucleus, which adds a checkpoint for screening out errors. Its continuity with the outer membrane of the ER shows that this membrane is homologous to the ER in evolutionary terms. The other three describe the nucleolus, the cell membrane and the DNA region of a prokaryotic cell.

questions.q: What is the nucleoid?
options: The place where the DNA sits in a bacterial cell, with no membrane around it.
The control room. It keeps the DNA and decides which genes are read.
The double membrane that encloses the nucleus.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
questions.why: Prokaryotic cells have no nuclear membrane, so the chromosome simply sits in a region of DNA in the cytoplasm with no boundary, and this region is called the nucleoid. It brings two consequences: transcription and translation can take place at the same time (a prokaryotic mRNA is picked up by a ribosome as soon as it appears), and DNA replication and transcription can proceed side by side, which is why bacteria can divide once every half hour or so. The other three describe the eukaryotic nucleus, the nuclear envelope and the nucleolus.

questions.q: A dense region inside the nucleus with no membrane around it, where rRNA is transcribed and assembled with proteins into ribosomal subunits that then travel through the nuclear pores to the cytoplasm; in cells that are making protein in bulk it is particularly large. What is this structure called?
options: The control room. It keeps the DNA and decides which genes are read.
The outer skin of the cell. A lipid bilayer that controls what enters and leaves and carries receptors.
The space between the two mitochondrial membranes, where protons accumulate to drive ATP synthase.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
questions.why: The nucleolus is a dense region inside the nucleus with no membrane around it, in which rRNA is transcribed and assembled with proteins into ribosomal subunits that are then carried out through the nuclear pores to the cytoplasm; its volume changes with the cell's need for protein synthesis, so in cells making protein in bulk the nucleolus is especially large. It appears on the organelle list in the second lecture alongside ribosome and the protein synthesis theme. The other three describe the nucleus, the cell membrane and the intermembrane space of the mitochondrion.

questions.q: What is the English name for the concept of the “control room: it keeps the DNA and decides which genes are read”?
options: Nucleolus
Nucleus
Nuclear envelope
Nucleoid
questions.why: The control room holds more than one ledger: it also has a selection mechanism. How tightly the chromatin is packed decides which stretch of door opens, transcription factors come in and bind the promoter, and enhancers reach round via DNA-bending proteins to deliver activators to the promoter. This is why the same DNA can express a completely different set of genes in a T cell and in a dendritic cell. The other three are respectively the nucleolus, the double membrane that encloses the nucleus and the DNA region of a prokaryotic cell.

questions.q: What is the English name for the concept of “a compartment inside the cell that does a single job, like a room in a factory”?
options: A small vesicle enclosed by a membrane, moving cargo between the compartments of the cell.
The network of fibres that gives the cell its shape, moves cargo, forms the spindle and pinches the cell in two.
A compartment inside the cell that does a single job, like a room in a factory.
The machine that reads mRNA and joins amino acids one after another.
questions.why: Their shared design principle is “separating mutually incompatible reactions”: wherever an acidic environment is needed, wherever oxidising and reducing conditions must be kept apart, wherever the DNA has to be walled off from other reactions, each gets its own room — the mitochondrion is the power station, the ER is the factory for protein synthesis, the Golgi apparatus is the packaging and sorting department, the lysosome is the recycling plant and the nucleus is the control room. The other three describe the vesicle, the fibrous network and the translation machine.

questions.q: Electrons travel along the respiratory chain (complexes I to IV) and the energy they release pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building an electrochemical gradient; the protons then flow back into the matrix along ATP synthase, driving it to assemble ADP and phosphate into ATP. This process is called ______.
options: The process by which mitochondria use oxygen to make most of the ATP.
The circular set of reactions in the mitochondrion that breaks fuel down and packs the energy into NADH and FADH₂.
The liquid interior of the mitochondrion, where the TCA cycle runs and mitochondrial DNA also lies.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
questions.why: Oxidative phosphorylation is exactly the process in which electrons pass along the respiratory chain, protons are pumped into the intermembrane space to build a gradient, and the protons then flow back into the matrix along ATP synthase to drive the assembly of ADP and phosphate into ATP; oxygen is the final electron acceptor and without it the whole chain stops, and the inner mitochondrial membrane is highly impermeable to protons, which is what holds the gradient in place. The comparison figures are these: a resting normal cell makes about 36 ATP aerobically and only 2 anaerobically, whereas a cancer cell makes only about 4 in either situation. The other three describe the TCA cycle, the mitochondrial matrix and the lysosome.

questions.q: What is the mechanism of action of palbociclib, and what does it do to the cell?
options: A protein whose level rises and falls during the cell cycle and switches on the matching CDK; it is the key, not the machine.
A family of inhibitory proteins that block CDK4/6 kinase and so stop the cell cycle.
The cell stops at a checkpoint without dividing; this is exactly what a CDK4/6 inhibitor causes.
A CDK4/6 inhibitor that stops the cell cycle in G1.
questions.why: For a cell to move from G1 into S phase, Cyclin D and CDK4/6 must phosphorylate pRb so that E2F can be released to switch on the S phase genes; palbociclib suppresses CDK4/6, so pRb stays under-phosphorylated, E2F is held down and the cell stays in G1 without entering S phase. This is a typical example of “using a drug to control the cell cycle”. The other three describe cyclin, the INK4 inhibitory proteins and cell cycle arrest.

questions.q: In the context of mitochondrial inheritance, what is the English word for “on the father's side”?
options: Maternal inheritance
paternal
Penetrance
Heteroplasmy
questions.why: In the setting of mitochondrial inheritance, paternal is used to describe the father's mitochondria: after fertilisation the sperm's mitochondria are tagged and destroyed, so all of the embryo's mitochondria come from the egg, that is, from the mother, and none of the father's mitochondria are left at all. Precisely for this reason the pattern is very recognisable on a pedigree: several consecutive generations, appearing in every generation, and passed down only through the mother. The other three are respectively the rule of maternal inheritance, penetrance and the mixed state of mtDNA.

questions.q: What is the English name for the concept of “what proportion of people carrying the same disease-causing mutation actually fall ill”?
options: Threshold effect
Heteroplasmy
Penetrance
Maternal inheritance
questions.why: Penetrance is what proportion of people carrying the mutation actually fall ill, and it is never 100%: some people become ill while others never show a symptom, because of other modifying effects of the gene, the tissue specificity of its expression and the environment. Incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity are two sides of the same coin, which also explains why patients on the same line of a pedigree can differ so much in severity. The other three are respectively the threshold effect, the mixed state of mtDNA and maternal inheritance.

questions.q: What are the structural and functional points of the plasma membrane?
options: The outer skin of the cell. A lipid bilayer that controls what enters and leaves and carries receptors.
The double membrane that encloses the nucleus.
The control room. It keeps the DNA and decides which genes are read.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
questions.why: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins and carbohydrate chains embedded in it. The phospholipids themselves do not let charged or large molecules through, so selective permeability depends on channels and transporters; receptors on the membrane carry messages in from outside the cell, while export pumps and transporters on the membrane carry substances out. Signal transduction, receptors, dimerisation and receptor occupancy all happen at the membrane. The other three describe the nuclear envelope, the nucleus and the nucleolus.

questions.q: ESCs and iPSCs belong to this differentiation potential, which can self-renew, proliferate indefinitely in the dish and be validated by the teratoma assay (growing tissue from all three germ layers after injection into an immunodeficient mouse); it is higher than multipotent and lower than totipotent. This potential is called ______.
options: Cells that can become several cell types, but only within the same family.
The mesoderm. It becomes muscle, bone and blood.
The ectoderm. It becomes the skin and the nervous system.
Cells that can become almost any cell type in the body.
questions.why: Pluripotent is higher than multipotent but still lower than totipotent (only totipotent can form a complete individual, placenta included); ESCs and iPSCs are both pluripotent, able to self-renew and to proliferate indefinitely in the dish. The standard validation is the teratoma assay: if the cells are injected into an immunodeficient mouse and form a tumour containing tissue from all three germ layers, they are proved to be pluripotent. The other three describe the range of multipotent and two germ layers.

questions.q: The protein that holds E2F down in G1 so that the S phase genes are not switched on is called ______.
options: A transcription factor normally held down by pRb; it is released when the cell is ready to divide.
The protein that holds the cell cycle in G1 until the cell is ready to replicate its DNA.
