Enzymes that cut other proteins; the caspase family carries out apoptosis.
The cell eats up the parts it does not need, in exchange for nutrients.
questions.why: pRb is the gate of the cell cycle: unphosphorylated pRb holds on to E2F, so this transcription factor cannot switch on the S phase genes and the cell stays in G1; when mitogenic signalling arrives, Cyclin D and CDK4/6 phosphorylate pRb, E2F is released and the cell enters S phase. The clinical extension is inhibitors such as palbociclib: they do not kill the cell, they simply hold it in G1 so that it never reaches S phase. The other three describe E2F, the enzyme that cleaves proteins and autophagy.

questions.q: How do prokaryotic cells differ from eukaryotic cells at the level of gene expression and regulation?
options: The place where the DNA sits in a bacterial cell, with no membrane around it.
Cells with a nucleus. Animals, plants, fungi and yeast are all eukaryotes.
Cells with no nucleus. Bacteria and archaea are all prokaryotes.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
questions.why: Without a nuclear membrane the chromosome lies directly in the nucleoid of the cytoplasm, and there are no membrane-bound organelles. This brings three practical consequences: transcription and translation can go on side by side in the same place (a prokaryotic mRNA is taken up by a ribosome as soon as it appears), proteins need no splicing and so there is no alternative splicing, and there is no post-transcriptional regulatory layer inside a nucleus; prokaryotes therefore reproduce quickly and have simple genomes. The other three describe the DNA region of prokaryotes, eukaryotic cells and the nucleolus.

questions.q: How does “quiescent” differ from “cell death”, and how do you experimentally bring cells into this state?
options: Quiescent cells are not dead; they have simply left the cell cycle, no longer divide but still keep their metabolism going, and dropping FBS from 10% to 0.5–1% to create serum starvation holds the cells in G1 so that they can be released synchronously.
Uncontrolled cell death after injury, in which the contents leak out and cause inflammation in the surrounding tissue.
Programmed cell death: the cell takes itself apart neatly instead of bursting.
The cell eats up the parts it does not need, in exchange for nutrients.
questions.why: Quiescent cells are not dead; they have simply left the cell cycle and no longer divide, while still keeping their metabolism going and still staying ready; G0 is not a stop on the cell cycle but a berth outside it, and when an external signal arrives (growth factors returning in the serum, for instance) the cell can re-enter G1. In both the second and the fourth lecture he uses serum starvation to hold cells in G0, and that 0.5–1% figure is there so that all the cells start from the same point. The other three describe necrosis, programmed cell death and autophagy.

questions.q: Labelling the two homologous chromosomes A, B, C and a, b, c, after the crossover there appear two chromatids carrying new combinations, A-B-c and a-b-C, while the A-B-C and a-b-c that took no part in the crossover are still there. What are these chromatids carrying new combinations after the crossover called?
options: The part of mitosis in which the chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles.
The deliberate exchange of DNA between homologous chromosomes in meiosis, which reshuffles genetic variation.
The special division in germ cells that produces four genetically different gametes.
Chromatids carrying new combinations after the crossover.
questions.why: Recombinant chromatids are precisely the chromatids carrying new combinations after the crossover (A-B-c and a-b-C); the first division of meiosis separates these combinations and the second hands them out to the four gametes, which is the source of diversity at the cellular level. The difference between M1 and M2 (2 normal and 2 abnormal against 1 normal and 3 abnormal) is exactly the first-tier question he named. The other three describe anaphase, the crossover in meiosis and the whole process of meiosis.

questions.q: What is the machine, made of a large and a small subunit, that grabs an mRNA, matches amino acids to its three-letter codons one by one and then joins the amino acids with peptide bonds called?
options: Ribosomal RNA, which makes up most of the ribosome and lines the mRNA up.
The machine that reads mRNA and joins amino acids one after another.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
questions.why: The ribosome is the translation machine of the factory: it grabs a copy of an mRNA (a photocopy of the recipe), matches amino acids to its three-letter codons one by one and joins them with peptide bonds, and the chain that results is the backbone of the protein, which only later folds into a working machine. The ribosome is itself neither an enzyme nor a template, and yet it is the single exit for all proteins, the last station on the “DNA → RNA → protein” production line. The other three describe rRNA, the nucleolus and the lysosome.

questions.q: How does RNA interference (RNAi) differ from CRISPR/Cas9 in the business of “switching a gene off”?
options: The machine that reads mRNA and joins amino acids one after another.
Ribosomal RNA, which makes up most of the ribosome and lines the mRNA up.
The older method of switching a gene off using small RNA molecules.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
questions.why: RNAi relies on the cell's own machinery: a designed double-stranded small RNA is put into the cell, RISC takes it apart into single strands and uses them for recognition, so the target mRNA is degraded or its translation is suppressed and protein output falls. Traditionally there are two approaches, siRNA and shRNA, and their shared weakness is that they knock down expression rather than switching the gene off completely. CRISPR/Cas9 has become the standard approach for gene knock-out and knock-in, and the older RNAi techniques have largely been replaced. The other three describe the ribosome, rRNA and the nucleolus.

questions.q: How does the division of labour between the rough ER and the smooth ER differ?
options: The part of the endoplasmic reticulum that carries ribosomes, where new proteins are made and folded.
The packaging room. It sorts finished proteins and sends them to their destinations.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
The space between the two mitochondrial membranes, where protons accumulate to drive ATP synthase.
questions.why: The rough ER is the protein factory: the ribosomes attached to its surface feed the growing peptide chain into the ER lumen, where chaperones help it fold and glycosylation is added on the spot, and it is released only once folding has succeeded, after which the finished protein is packaged into a transport vesicle and sent to the Golgi apparatus. The difference between rough and smooth lies only in whether there are ribosomes on the surface: where there are, it is rough and handles proteins; where there are not, it is smooth and handles lipids. The other three describe the Golgi apparatus, the lysosome and the intermembrane space of the mitochondrion.

questions.q: What is the RNA called that is the most abundant component of the ribosome, forms the large and small subunits together with proteins, and catalyses peptide bond formation, making the ribosome essentially a ribozyme?
options: The machine that reads mRNA and joins amino acids one after another.
The control room. It keeps the DNA and decides which genes are read.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
Ribosomal RNA, which makes up most of the ribosome and lines the mRNA up.
questions.why: The function of rRNA is not to act as a template but as machinery: the reaction centre that catalyses peptide bond formation is made chiefly of rRNA, which means the ribosome is essentially a ribozyme; at the same time it positions the mRNA correctly, so that the three-letter codons line up exactly with the anticodons of the tRNA. It is also the emblem of the RNA world idea that “RNA can be its own catalyst”; the ribosomal subunits are 70S in bacteria and 80S in the eukaryotic cytoplasm. The other three describe the ribosome, the nucleus and the nucleolus.

questions.q: What is the part of the cell cycle in which DNA is replicated in full once and the DNA content climbs from 2N to 4N called?
options: The checkpoint phase after DNA replication is complete and before the cell divides.
The part of the cell cycle in which DNA is replicated.
The growth phase of the cell cycle, before DNA replication.
The resting branch of the cell cycle, where the cell stays when it is alive but not dividing.
questions.why: S phase is the synthesis phase, in which DNA is replicated in full once and the content climbs from 2N to 4N; the replication itself opens out at the origins into thousands of replication bubbles, each with a replication fork running on either side, one leading strand made continuously and the other lagging strand made in pieces as Okazaki fragments. S phase is also the period most easily interrupted by DNA damage, because a replication fork that collides with damaged DNA stalls, which is why the DNA repair pathways matter so much in S/G2. The other three describe G2, G1 and G0.

questions.q: What is the English name of the manoeuvre of “dropping the serum in the medium from 10% to 0.5–1% so that the cells stop in G1”?
options: Cell cycle arrest
Quiescent
Serum starvation
Checkpoint
questions.why: Serum starvation is the manoeuvre of taking FBS (fetal bovine serum) away: FBS is the nutrient supply that feeds the cells in the medium and it contains growth factors, and once it is removed the cells lose the signal to “keep dividing” and stop quietly in G1; when the serum is put back, all the cells leave G1 and enter S phase at the same moment. The whole procedure is called cell-cycle synchronisation, and it gives replication experiments and drug experiments a clean starting line. The other three are respectively cell cycle arrest, the quiescent state and the checkpoint.

questions.q: What is the part of the endoplasmic reticulum that carries no ribosomes, synthesises phospholipids and steroids, metabolises drugs and detoxifies, and also takes part in the storage and release of calcium ions called?
options: The part of the endoplasmic reticulum with no ribosomes attached, which makes lipids.
The part of the endoplasmic reticulum that carries ribosomes, where new proteins are made and folded.
The packaging room. It sorts finished proteins and sends them to their destinations.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
questions.why: The smooth ER carries no ribosomes; it synthesises lipids (phospholipids and steroids), metabolises drugs and detoxifies, and also takes part in the storage and release of calcium ions. The division of labour with the rough ER is very clean: rough makes protein, smooth makes lipid, and the plasma membrane is itself a phospholipid bilayer, so when we say “the cell makes its own membrane” we are really talking about the smooth ER. The other three describe the rough ER, the Golgi apparatus and the lysosome.

questions.q: What are the two capacities of a stem cell, and what is its classification hierarchy?
options: The mesoderm. It becomes muscle, bone and blood.
The ectoderm. It becomes the skin and the nervous system.
The endoderm. It becomes the gut lining and the lung.
A cell that can copy itself and can also become a more specialised cell.
questions.why: A stem cell has two capacities: self-renewal, and differentiation into more specialised cells. His classification covers ESC (embryonic stem cells, pluripotent, capable of unlimited self-renewal), adult stem cells (the haematopoietic stem cell, for instance) and iPSC; the degree of differentiation is a continuum: totipotent → pluripotent → multipotent → unipotent. He stresses that the value of iPSC lies in solving two problems at once: sidestepping the ethical controversy around embryonic stem cells, and making disease models possible, by deriving iPSCs from a patient's own cells and differentiating them into cardiomyocytes to test cardiotoxicity. The other three describe the three germ layers.

questions.q: Once the extrinsic pathway of apoptosis has been triggered, caspase-8 cleaves bid and the fragment that is cut out travels to the mitochondrion and promotes the release of cytochrome c, connecting the extrinsic route to the mitochondrial one. What is this fragment called?
options: The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
The fragment cut out of bid by caspase-8, which connects the extrinsic pathway of apoptosis to the mitochondrion.
The dense region inside the nucleus where the components of the ribosome are made.
The outer skin of the cell. A lipid bilayer that controls what enters and leaves and carries receptors.
questions.why: tbid is the fragment cut out of bid by caspase-8: once caspase-8 has been activated it cleaves not only caspase-3 but bid as well; the tbid that is cut out goes to the mitochondrion, prompts the release of cytochrome c and the assembly of the apoptosome, so that the extrinsic and intrinsic pathways meet on the same execution programme and both finally converge on caspase-3. The other three describe the lysosome, the nucleolus and the cell membrane.

questions.q: What is the circular set of reactions that turns round in the mitochondrial matrix, oxidising the carbons of acetyl-CoA step by step into carbon dioxide and storing the released electrons in NADH and FADH₂ called?
options: The process by which mitochondria use oxygen to make most of the ATP.
The liquid interior of the mitochondrion, where the TCA cycle runs and mitochondrial DNA also lies.
The circular set of reactions in the mitochondrion that breaks fuel down and packs the energy into NADH and FADH₂.
The folds that the inner mitochondrial membrane makes inwards, on which the ATP-making machinery sits.
questions.why: The TCA cycle (citric acid cycle, Krebs cycle) oxidises the carbons of acetyl-CoA step by step into carbon dioxide and stores the released electrons in carriers such as NADH and FADH₂; these carriers then pass the electrons into the electron transport chain and finally hand them to oxygen, and the proton gradient built up along the way drives ATP synthase to make ATP. For a cancer cell this whole line is the one that has been given up: sending 85% of the pyruvate to lactate is precisely what stops it entering the TCA cycle. The other three describe oxidative phosphorylation, the mitochondrial matrix and the folds of the inner membrane.

questions.q: Why is the teratoma assay called the gold standard for validating pluripotency?
options: The gold standard for judging whether cells are really pluripotent: inject them into a mouse and see whether tissue from all three germ layers grows.
The mesoderm. It becomes muscle, bone and blood.
The ectoderm. It becomes the skin and the nervous system.
The endoderm. It becomes the gut lining and the lung.
questions.why: The teratoma assay injects the cells under test into an immunodeficient mouse; if they really are pluripotent they grow in vivo into a tumour containing tissue from all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm), and the histology shows cartilage, CNS, muscle, adipose and epithelium, even hair, sebum and a tooth. This is far more convincing than “it looks like an embryonic cell”: it is a functional proof. The other three describe the three germ layers themselves.

questions.q: What does the threshold effect of mitochondrial disease mean?
options: The state in which normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA are mixed together inside one cell.
Every copy of mitochondrial DNA in a cell is identical, whether normal or mutant.
The proportion of people carrying the mutation who actually develop disease. It is never 100%.

Carrying mutant mtDNA does not mean you will fall ill: symptoms appear only when the proportion of mutants passes the tolerance limit set for that tissue; skeletal muscle, which has a high energy demand, has a low threshold and is affected first, while hearing, with a low demand, has a high threshold and is affected later.
questions.why: Having normal and mutant mtDNA side by side in one person is called heteroplasmy, but carrying a mutation is not the same as being ill: the proportion of mutants has to pass the threshold set for that tissue before symptoms appear. His body map lists the organs affected, from neurodegeneration, epilepsy and deafness to cardiomyopathy, liver disease, kidney disease, diabetes and infertility — an extremely wide range. The other three describe the mixed state of mtDNA, the state in which everything is identical, and penetrance.

questions.q: What is the English name of the “extrinsic ligand that activates caspase-8 after binding a death receptor on the cell surface, and thereby activates caspase-3”?
options: TRAILR2
TRAIL
Caspase
Apoptosis
questions.why: When TRAIL binds the death receptor, caspase-8 is lit up and then activates caspase-3; at the same time caspase-8 cleaves bid into tbid, carrying the signal into the mitochondrion and merging with the intrinsic pathway. Its pharmacological attraction is that it is far less toxic to normal cells than to tumour cells, which is why it is used as one end of a bispecific antibody — BI 905711 hits TRAILR2 and CDH17 at the same time. The other three are respectively the receptor for TRAIL, the enzyme that cleaves proteins and programmed cell death.

questions.q: What is the English name of the receptor for TRAIL, which is also DR5?
options: TRAIL
CDH17 (Cadherin-17)
TRAILR2
Caspase
questions.why: When TRAILR2 binds TRAIL it starts the death receptor pathway. His own bispecific antibody BI 905711 ties TRAILR2 (the death receptor on the tumour) to CDH17 (the cancer cell surface protein he has studied for twenty years) on the same molecule, and attacks only when both appear together, which is the AND-gate. The other three are respectively the TRAIL ligand, CDH17 and the enzyme that cleaves proteins.

questions.q: What is the English name of the shipping end of the Golgi apparatus (the side facing the plasma membrane, where processed proteins are packaged into secretory vesicles)?
options: Trans face
Cis face
Rough ER
Golgi apparatus
questions.why: The trans face is the shipping end of the Golgi apparatus: fully processed proteins are packaged here into secretory vesicles for the plasma membrane, whereas the cis face is the receiving end, where transport vesicles dock and deliver their cargo for the Golgi to process and sort step by step. The division of labour among the enzymes also follows position: the glycosylation steps are spread between the cis and the trans face, with different glycosyltransferases housed in different cisternae, like a conveyor belt with assigned stations. The other three are respectively the receiving end, the rough ER and the Golgi apparatus itself.

questions.q: What is a transport vesicle, and what delivers its cargo to the right place?
options: The control room. It keeps the DNA and decides which genes are read.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
The packaging room. It sorts finished proteins and sends them to their destinations.
A small membrane bubble that carries cargo from one compartment to the next.
questions.why: A vesicle is a small bubble wrapped in a membrane, like the delivery carts that move around inside a factory, and it unloads by fusing with the target membrane: the rough ER loads new proteins into a transport vesicle and sends it to the cis face of the Golgi, and after the Golgi has processed and sorted them it sends secretory vesicles out from the trans face to the plasma membrane, where fusion releases the protein outside the cell or embeds it in the membrane as a receptor. Direction is controlled by Rab proteins and the SNARE complex. The other three describe the nucleus, the lysosome and the Golgi apparatus.

questions.q: What types does the general term vesicle cover, and how is the direction best remembered?
options: The packaging room. It sorts finished proteins and sends them to their destinations.
A small vesicle enclosed by a membrane, moving cargo between the compartments of the cell.
The power station. It makes most of the ATP, controls apoptosis, and carries its own DNA.
The acidic recycling and processing plant inside the cell.
questions.why: Vesicle is the collective name for all the transport tools inside the cell: transport vesicles (ER to Golgi), secretory vesicles (Golgi to plasma membrane, for secretion), and endosomes/lysosomes (which take in foreign material and break it down); each is wrapped in a membrane homologous to the plasma membrane and carries the cargo inside, and vesicles travel along the microfilaments and microtubules. The direction to remember is: rough ER → transport vesicle → Golgi cis face → trans face → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane. The other three describe the Golgi apparatus, the mitochondrion and the lysosome.

questions.q: Which four factors are needed to reprogramme fibroblasts into iPSCs?
options: The receiving end of the Golgi apparatus, where incoming vesicles dock.
The ectoderm. It becomes the skin and the nervous system.
Oct3/4, Sox2, c-Myc and Klf4 — the four factors that reprogramme fibroblasts into iPSCs.
The mesoderm. It becomes muscle, bone and blood.
questions.why: In 2006 Takahashi and Yamanaka showed that expressing the four factors Oct3/4, Sox2, c-Myc and Klf4 together is enough to return a differentiated somatic cell (a fibroblast) to a pluripotent state and produce iPSCs. The significance of reprogramming is enormous: it bypasses the ethical controversy over embryonic stem cells, and it makes it possible to make iPSCs from a patient's own cells and then differentiate them into cardiomyocytes to test cardiotoxicity. The other three describe the receiving end of the Golgi apparatus and two germ layers.
